Biology 30 · Chapter 18

Molecular Genetics

DNA stores genetic information. Cells copy DNA and use its instructions to make RNA and proteins. Follow the information through these processes and explain how a change in DNA can affect a protein.

12 teaching topics1 integrated review13 required checks
Begin Topic 1

How genetic information works

DNA stores genetic information. Cells copy DNA and use its instructions to make RNA and proteins. Follow the information through these processes and explain how a change in DNA can affect a protein.

By the end of this chapter, I can:

  • I can connect experimental evidence with DNA’s hereditary role.
  • I can use structure and direction to explain replication and gene expression.
  • I can solve explicit DNA, RNA and protein sequence problems.
  • I can interpret mutations and genetic technologies without exceeding the evidence.

Work through the topics, complete the required checks, and use the figures and practice activities to review. Your saved responses and vocabulary work are in Process Collection.

What made DNA a stronger explanation of heredity than protein?

Chapter 18 · printed pp. 624–628

Open p. 624 · Open p. 628

Key terms: · · ·

Vocabulary help

Key terms

Words for this lesson

Use these definitions when you need help with a term.

A heritable change associated with a cell taking up external genetic material.
Material that stores and transmits inherited biological information.
A detectable radioactive label used to follow the movement of material.
A comparison designed to distinguish explanations by changing a relevant factor while keeping others comparable.

Griffith established a transferable change

Griffith studied bacteria with different disease-causing properties. Live non-virulent bacteria could acquire a heritable virulent trait when mixed with heat-killed virulent bacteria. Material from the killed cells had changed the living bacterial lineage.

This result supported . It did not identify the transforming substance. DNA and protein were among the candidates, so the next question was which component was necessary for the change.

Remove a candidate and test the effect

Avery, MacLeod and McCarty studied transforming preparations and used treatments aimed at different components. When DNA was destroyed, transforming activity was lost. Comparable treatments directed at other components did not remove activity in the same way.

This was stronger evidence for DNA because the experiment connected an intervention with the loss of a measured function. The useful comparison is not simply that DNA was present. It is that destroying DNA disrupted transformation under the experimental conditions.

Trace the material entering infected cells

Hershey and Chase used bacteriophages, viruses that infect bacteria. In separate preparations, phosphorus-32 labelled viral DNA and sulfur-35 labelled viral protein. After infection, they separated much of the external phage material from the bacterial cells.

The DNA label was associated much more strongly with the infected cells than the external protein label. This supported DNA as the material entering the cells and directing viral production in that system.

Together the experiments built a case for DNA as . They did not by themselves explain its double-helical structure or every step of gene expression. Match each scientist with the specific question their evidence addressed.

Worked example

Separate observation from conclusion

A transforming preparation stops transforming bacteria after a DNA-destroying enzyme is added; other enzyme treatments retain activity.

  1. Identify the measured outcome: transformation of the bacterial lineage.
  2. Identify the intervention: destroying DNA in the preparation.
  3. Compare with other treatments so that enzyme addition alone is not the explanation.
  4. Conclude that intact DNA is necessary for transforming activity in this assay.
  5. Do not claim that this experiment determined the sequence of the entire bacterial genome.

Practise with support

Apply the explanation

Try both questions. Use the hint to revise your thinking after an incorrect answer.

Stop and think

Try this before opening the explanation

Does a successful experiment answer every question about heredity?

Show the explanation

No. Its conclusion is limited by the intervention, controls and outcome measured.

Chapter 18 · printed pp. 628–631

Open p. 628 · Open p. 631

Key terms: · · ·

Vocabulary help

Key terms

Words for this lesson

Use these definitions when you need help with a term.

A nucleic-acid subunit containing a sugar, phosphate and nitrogenous base.
Specific pairing of bases across nucleic-acid strands.
Oriented in opposite directions.
The equality of A with T and C with G in standard double-stranded DNA.

Build a nucleotide before building a helix

DNA is a polymer: a long chain made from subunits. Each DNA nucleotide contains deoxyribose sugar, a phosphate group and a nitrogenous base. The four bases are adenine, thymine, cytosine and guanine, abbreviated A, T, C and G.

Sugars and phosphates form the backbone of each strand. Bases project inward and pair with bases on the other strand. Covalent bonds hold the backbone together; hydrogen bonds connect complementary bases across the strands. These are different connections and perform different structural roles.

Pairing and direction are separate rules

In the standard double-stranded DNA model, A pairs with T and C pairs with G. A and G are double-ring purines; C and T are single-ring pyrimidines. A purine paired with a pyrimidine helps maintain a consistent width.

The strands are . If an upper strand is written 5′-ATGC-3′, its aligned partner is 3′-TACG-5′. If you must report that partner in the 5′ to 3′ direction, reverse the displayed order: 5′-GCAT-3′.

The numbers identify positions in the sugar and therefore strand orientation. They do not identify the first and third bases in a codon. Direction becomes essential when interpreting replication and transcription.

Use proportions without assuming equal amounts

Chargaff’s observations supported equality between A and T, and between C and G, in double-stranded DNA. If A accounts for 30% of all bases, T is 30%, leaving 40% for C and G together. Each is therefore 20%.

Franklin’s X-ray diffraction work provided important structural evidence. Watson and Crick developed a double-helix model consistent with that evidence and the base relationships. Structure, chemical composition and inherited function were connected by different lines of investigation.

Do not apply equal A/T proportions to every single strand by itself. The equalities arise from the complementary double-stranded molecule.

Worked example

Write a complement with its direction

An upper strand is 5′-AAGTC-3′. Write the aligned complementary strand and then write that partner 5′ to 3′.

  1. Pair A with T, A with T, G with C, T with A and C with G.
  2. The aligned partner is 3′-TTCAG-5′.
  3. To report the partner 5′ to 3′, read it from its 5′ end: 5′-GACTT-3′.
  4. Check that the strands are complementary when aligned antiparallel.

Practise with support

Apply the explanation

Try both questions. Use the hint to revise your thinking after an incorrect answer.

Stop and think

Try this before opening the explanation

Are the two aligned DNA strands identical?

Show the explanation

No. They are complementary and run in opposite directions.

Chapter 18 · printed pp. 631–635

Open p. 631 · Open p. 635

Key terms: · · ·

Vocabulary help

Key terms

Words for this lesson

Use these definitions when you need help with a term.

Replication producing DNA molecules with one parental strand and one newly synthesized strand.
An enzyme that extends a new DNA strand by adding nucleotides to its 3′ end.
A short newly synthesized DNA segment on the lagging strand.
An enzyme that seals breaks in the sugar-phosphate backbone.

Use each parental strand as a template

Replication begins at an origin and opens a region of the DNA. Helicase separates the paired strands by disrupting their hydrogen-bond interactions. It does not cut each strand’s sugar-phosphate backbone into small pieces.

Each parental strand provides a template for a complementary new strand. The two resulting DNA molecules each contain one old strand and one new strand. This is .

Meselson and Stahl followed DNA density after cells moved from a heavy-nitrogen medium to a light-nitrogen medium. The first generation produced intermediate-density DNA. In the second, intermediate and light DNA appeared. This pattern supported semiconservative replication over the alternatives tested.

A primer provides a starting point

cannot begin a new strand from nothing. Primase makes a short RNA primer that supplies a starting 3′ end. DNA polymerase then extends from that end with complementary DNA nucleotides.

New DNA is always synthesized 5′ to 3′. Because the parental templates run in opposite directions, their new strands cannot both follow the moving replication fork continuously.

The leading strand is synthesized continuously toward the fork. The lagging strand is made in Okazaki fragments, each extending 5′ to 3′ away from the fork as additional template is exposed. Each fragment requires a primer.

Finish the backbone and check the result

RNA primers are removed and replaced with DNA through the replication machinery. seals the remaining backbone breaks between adjacent segments. Proofreading and repair reduce errors, although some DNA changes can persist.

Use the enzyme names to explain different jobs: helicase opens, primase starts, DNA polymerase extends, and ligase joins. Do not use the word “copies” as if one enzyme performs every part.

Replication increases DNA amount but does not by itself separate sister chromatids into daughter cells. Cell division is a later process.

Worked example

Interpret the second generation

Cells with fully heavy-labelled DNA replicate twice in light-nitrogen medium. Predict the DNA types under semiconservative replication.

  1. After the first replication, every molecule has one heavy parental strand and one light new strand.
  2. Each hybrid molecule then separates its strands for the second replication.
  3. The heavy strand produces another hybrid; the light strand produces a fully light molecule.
  4. The expected second-generation molecules are half hybrid and half light, with no fully heavy molecules.

Practise with support

Apply the explanation

Try both questions. Use the hint to revise your thinking after an incorrect answer.

Stop and think

Try this before opening the explanation

Does helicase normally cut the DNA backbone to expose the bases?

Show the explanation

No. It separates the paired strands while their backbones remain intact.

Chapter 18 · printed pp. 636–637

Open p. 636 · Open p. 637

Key terms: · · ·

Vocabulary help

Key terms

Words for this lesson

Use these definitions when you need help with a term.

The use of genetic information to produce a functional RNA or protein product.
RNA that carries a sequence used to direct protein synthesis.
RNA that helps match an mRNA codon with its corresponding amino acid.
RNA that forms structural and catalytic parts of ribosomes.

A shared genome does not require identical activity

Many nucleated somatic cells contain essentially the same inherited genome, yet muscle, nerve and other cells perform different tasks. They express different sets of genes and produce different amounts of particular products.

is not the same as changing the DNA sequence. A cell can change which genes are active without replacing every gene it contains. Some genes produce functional RNA rather than a protein.

Separate the molecules and their jobs

DNA generally stores information in a double-stranded molecule using deoxyribose and the bases A, T, C and G. RNA uses ribose and uracil, U, instead of thymine. RNA is usually single-stranded but can fold through base pairing within the molecule.

For a protein-coding gene, transcription produces RNA from a DNA template. Translation uses the sequence to assemble amino acids into a polypeptide. The commonly taught information pathway is DNA → RNA → protein.

Messenger RNA carries the sequence, brings matched amino acids, and forms part of the ribosome’s structure and catalytic machinery. These RNA types have different roles even though all are nucleic acids.

Locate the processes in a eukaryotic cell

For the nuclear genes considered here, transcription occurs in the nucleus. The RNA is processed, and mature mRNA can leave through nuclear pores. Translation occurs at ribosomes in the cytoplasm, including ribosomes associated with rough endoplasmic reticulum.

A protein’s amino-acid sequence influences how it folds and functions. A different sequence may change that function, but not every sequence difference has an equally large effect.

Do not describe non-protein-coding DNA as automatically useless. Some sequences regulate expression, and some genes produce functional RNAs. This chapter focuses on protein synthesis without claiming that it explains every DNA function.

Worked example

Same inherited instructions, different output

A muscle cell produces much more of a muscle-associated protein than another nucleated somatic cell.

  1. Both cells can carry the relevant DNA sequence.
  2. Different regulation changes which genes are transcribed and how much product is made.
  3. mRNA and translation connect the expressed gene with the protein output.
  4. The observation does not require one cell to have lost every unused gene.

Practise with support

Apply the explanation

Try both questions. Use the hint to revise your thinking after an incorrect answer.

Stop and think

Try this before opening the explanation

Does every functional gene have to encode a protein?

Show the explanation

No. Some genes produce functional RNA products.

Key terms: · · ·

Vocabulary help

Key terms

Words for this lesson

Use these definitions when you need help with a term.

The DNA strand read by RNA polymerase to construct complementary RNA.
The DNA strand whose 5′ to 3′ sequence matches the RNA sequence apart from T versus U.
An enzyme that synthesizes RNA using a DNA template.
Removal of introns and joining of retained exon sequences in a pre-mRNA.

Read the template, not the label you remember

binds at a gene’s regulatory starting region and opens a short DNA region. It reads the in the 3′ to 5′ direction while building complementary RNA 5′ to 3′. Only one DNA strand serves as the template for a particular transcript.

A on the DNA template pairs with U in RNA; T pairs with A; C pairs with G; G pairs with C. The other DNA strand is called the because its 5′ to 3′ sequence matches the RNA sequence except that DNA has T and RNA has U.

For example, template 3′-TAC GGA-5′ produces 5′-AUG CCU-3′. Its coding DNA partner is 5′-ATG CCT-3′. Identify which strand you have before deciding whether to complement or simply replace T with U.

An RNA message is not a new DNA helix

Transcription copies the information of a selected DNA region into RNA. The DNA strands close behind the enzyme and the RNA separates. It does not copy the entire genome in the same way as S-phase replication.

Because one continuous RNA molecule is synthesized from one template, transcription does not require a leading strand, lagging strand or Okazaki fragments. Those terms belong to DNA replication at a fork.

Process the eukaryotic transcript

A newly made eukaryotic pre-mRNA is commonly processed before export. Introns are removed, and exons are joined. A cap and a poly-A tail help protect the message and support its use by the cell.

Introns are removed from the RNA, not normally cut out of the genomic DNA during this processing step. Exons are the portions retained in the mature RNA; some retained sequence is not translated.

Once processing is complete, the mature message can leave the nucleus. Keep transcription, RNA processing and translation as distinct steps even though they contribute to one overall gene-expression pathway.

Worked example

Choose the correct conversion

You are given coding DNA 5′-ATG TTT TAA-3′. Find the corresponding mRNA.

  1. Identify the supplied strand as coding DNA, already written 5′ to 3′.
  2. Keep its base order and replace T with U.
  3. The mRNA is 5′-AUG UUU UAA-3′.
  4. Check against the template: 3′-TAC AAA ATT-5′ would give the same mRNA by complementary pairing.

Practise with support

Apply the explanation

Try both questions. Use the hint to revise your thinking after an incorrect answer.

Stop and think

Try this before opening the explanation

Does splicing normally delete introns from the inherited DNA molecule?

Show the explanation

No. It removes them from the RNA transcript.

Key terms: · · ·

Vocabulary help

Key terms

Words for this lesson

Use these definitions when you need help with a term.

A three-nucleotide sequence in mRNA interpreted during translation.
A tRNA triplet that pairs antiparallel with an mRNA codon.
The grouping of a nucleotide sequence into successive triplets for translation.
An mRNA codon signalling termination rather than an amino acid.

Read the message in triplets

A ribosome reads in successive three- codons. Each amino-acid specifies one amino acid in the standard code. Several different codons can specify the same amino acid; this redundancy does not mean one codon specifies several amino acids at once.

AUG commonly acts as a start codon and specifies methionine. Starting at the correct AUG establishes the . A sequence written for codon practice may instead be identified as an internal coding segment; follow that instruction rather than assuming every short fragment contains the beginning of a full gene.

Match and join

A carries an amino acid and has an that can pair with a complementary mRNA codon. The strands pair . For mRNA 5′-AUG-3′, an aligned anticodon is 3′-UAC-5′.

Ribosomes contain and proteins. As matching tRNAs enter and the ribosome moves along the mRNA, amino acids are linked by peptide bonds. The growing chain is a polypeptide, which can later fold and undergo additional processing.

The mRNA is not physically converted into protein. It is read as information while amino acids are assembled from a separate supply.

Stop at the signal and use the right table

UAA, UAG and UGA are stop codons in the standard code. A release factor helps terminate translation and release the chain. A does not recruit a tRNA carrying a “stop amino acid.”

Always use the mRNA codon, written 5′ to 3′, when looking up an amino acid. Convert a DNA template or anticodon first. A protein chain is described by amino-acid order; it does not have DNA-style 5′ and 3′ ends.

Use the codon reference included in this course. It provides the information needed for sequence questions without requiring a separate data booklet.

Worked example

Translate a complete short message

A coding message is 5′-AUG UUU GGC UAA-3′. Translate from the first AUG.

  1. AUG establishes the frame and contributes methionine (Met).
  2. UUU specifies phenylalanine (Phe).
  3. GGC specifies glycine (Gly).
  4. UAA terminates translation and contributes no amino acid.
  5. The chain is Met–Phe–Gly: three amino acids, not four.

Vocabulary help

Key terms

Words for this lesson

Use these definitions when you need help with a term.

The complementary strand reported in the opposite displayed order so that it is written 5′ to 3′.
The ordered amino acids in a peptide or protein.
A sequence region interpreted as codons in a specified reading frame.
Checking molecule identity, direction, pairing and code interpretation against explicit rules.

Write the problem’s identity line first

Before changing any letters, write four things: the supplied molecule, its strand identity if it is DNA, the displayed direction, and the requested output. “DNA” alone is insufficient when a question expects an unambiguous sequence.

For coding DNA written 5′ to 3′, replace T with U. For template DNA written 3′ to 5′, construct the complementary RNA from left to right. For template DNA written 5′ to 3′, the RNA must be constructed from the template’s opposite end and reported 5′ to 3′.

Keep the direction labels visible until the final check. Removing them early is a common reason for getting correct pairings in the wrong order.

Establish the frame before translating

For a complete simplified message, begin at the specified start AUG and stop at the first in-frame . Divide the sequence into triplets only after establishing the start. Bases before the start are not automatically translated.

For an explicitly stated internal , use the supplied . Such an exercise can ask for amino-acid identities without including the beginning of the protein. Do not invent a start or stop that the question does not provide.

A stretch coding for five amino acids contains fifteen coding nucleotides. An additional stop requires three more nucleotides but does not add an amino acid. State whether the question includes that signal.

Check the result in both directions

Compare each RNA base with the template and compare the RNA with the coding DNA partner. Then consult the codon table one triplet at a time. Check that a stop has not been counted as an amino acid.

Several RNA sequences can produce the same peptide because of code redundancy. From a protein sequence alone, you can often give a possible RNA sequence, but not a unique original sequence.

The short sequences in these exercises are constructed teaching examples, not complete human genes or laboratory protocols.

Worked example

Handle a template supplied 5′ to 3′

Template DNA is 5′-TTA CCC TTT CAT-3′. Find mRNA 5′ to 3′ and translate from its start.

  1. Reverse the template’s displayed order before constructing the 5′ to 3′ RNA.
  2. Complement the reversed template: the RNA is 5′-AUG AAA GGG UAA-3′.
  3. Group from AUG: AUG / AAA / GGG / UAA.
  4. The chain is Met–Lys–Gly; UAA stops translation.
  5. Check that the RNA pairs antiparallel with the original template.

Chapter 18 · printed pp. 643–647

Open p. 643 · Open p. 647

Key terms: · · ·

Vocabulary help

Key terms

Words for this lesson

Use these definitions when you need help with a term.

A persistent change in a DNA sequence.
A coding substitution that leaves the specified amino acid unchanged.
A coding change that introduces a premature stop codon.
A shift in reading frame caused by an insertion or deletion not divisible by three in a coding region.

Locate the change in DNA

A is a persistent DNA sequence change. It may arise from replication errors or DNA damage that is not accurately repaired. An error during transcription or translation can alter an individual product without changing the DNA template itself.

A substitution replaces one base with another. In a coding region, its consequence depends on the resulting . A leaves the amino acid unchanged; a missense substitution changes an amino acid; a introduces a premature stop.

Check the code rather than guessing severity

Consider the internal mRNA CAG UUA CCC. It specifies Gln–Leu–Pro. Changing UUA to UUG still gives leucine, a silent substitution. Changing UUA to UCA gives serine, a missense change. Changing it to UAA creates a stop signal.

The size of a change in DNA does not by itself determine the effect on the organism. Protein location, function, remaining sequence and other biological factors matter. A missense change can be important or relatively minor; a premature stop can remove a critical region.

Track the frame and the lineage

An insertion or deletion of one shifts the downstream triplet grouping. Insertions or deletions not divisible by three can therefore cause a in a translated region. Removing exactly three bases may remove an amino acid without shifting later codons.

A somatic mutation occurs in a body-cell lineage. It can affect that organism and descendant cells without usually entering its gametes. A germ-line mutation can be transmitted if it is present in a gamete that contributes to an offspring. “Can be inherited” does not mean every offspring receives it.

Mutations create new sequence variants. Selection and other population processes determine how their frequencies change; organisms do not produce the exact mutation they need on demand.

Worked example

Classify the actual coding effect

An internal coding RNA sequence changes from 5′-CAG UUA CCC-3′ to 5′-CAG UUG CCC-3′ as a result of a DNA substitution.

  1. The changed codon is UUA → UUG.
  2. Use the mRNA table: both specify leucine.
  3. The peptide remains Gln–Leu–Pro.
  4. Classify the coding substitution as silent rather than assuming every base change alters the protein.

Practise with support

Apply the explanation

Try both questions. Use the hint to revise your thinking after an incorrect answer.

Try this before opening the explanation

Show the explanation

No. It can change the reproductive success of variants already present or arising independently.

Chapter 18 · printed pp. 647–651

Open p. 647 · Open p. 651

Key terms: · · ·

Vocabulary help

Key terms

Words for this lesson

Use these definitions when you need help with a term.

The production of new combinations of genetic material.
Transfer of genetic material between bacterial cells through direct contact.
Transfer of bacterial genetic material mediated by a virus.
DNA located in mitochondria rather than in the nuclear chromosomes.

Separate new sequences from new combinations

A can create a new allele. Recombination can bring existing alleles together in new arrangements. During meiosis, crossing over exchanges corresponding DNA between non-sister chromatids, and independent assortment distributes homologues into gametes.

Random fertilization adds another level of combination. An offspring can therefore differ from both parents without every difference requiring a new mutation. Keep the origin of a sequence variant separate from its reassortment.

Bacteria exchange genetic material in several ways

Bacteria normally reproduce by binary fission, but they can also acquire DNA from other sources. involves uptake of external DNA. involves direct contact and transfer, often including plasmids. involves a virus carrying bacterial genetic material.

These mechanisms can introduce traits into a bacterial lineage. They are not the same as mitosis or the production and fusion of animal gametes. The important question is how the DNA enters and how it can persist in descendants.

A transferred sequence must be maintained and expressed in an appropriate context to affect a phenotype. Detecting DNA outside a cell is not enough to establish a stable inherited change.

Mitochondrial DNA records a particular lineage

Mitochondria contain their own DNA, consistent with their evolutionary origin through endosymbiosis. In the usual human model, mitochondrial inheritance is predominantly maternal because the egg contributes the mitochondria retained in the embryo.

Comparing can inform relationships along maternal lineages. It does not represent the entire nuclear genome or all branches of ancestry. Similarity of a short sequence is evidence to interpret, not a complete family history.

Do not assume mitochondrial variants are always harmless. Like other sequence changes, their effects depend on the genes and biological processes involved.

Worked example

Identify the route of transfer

A bacterium acquires DNA carried by a bacteriophage, and its descendants retain an associated trait.

  1. The carrier is a virus, which identifies transduction.
  2. Retention in descendants supports a heritable genetic change rather than temporary external contamination.
  3. This is distinct from transformation by free DNA or conjugation through contact.
  4. The transferred allele may already have existed in another bacterium; transfer need not create it by mutation.

Show the explanation

No. New allele combinations can arise without changing chromosome number.

Read the explanation

Bacteria normally reproduce by binary fission, but they can also acquire DNA from other sources. Transformation involves uptake of external DNA. Conjugation involves direct contact and transfer, often including plasmids. Transduction involves a virus carrying bacterial genetic material. These mechanisms can introduce traits into a bacterial lineage. They are not the same as mitosis or the production and fusion of animal gametes. The important question is how the DNA enters and how it can persist in descendants. A transferred sequence must be maintained and expressed in an appropriate context to affect a phenotype. Detecting DNA outside a cell is not enough to establish a stable inherited change.

What must happen for a transferred gene to produce a useful product?

Chapter 18 · printed pp. 652–655

Open p. 652 · Open p. 655

Key terms: · · ·

Vocabulary help

Key terms

Words for this lesson

Use these definitions when you need help with a term.

A DNA molecule assembled from genetic material from different sources.
An enzyme that cuts DNA at particular recognition sequences.
A small DNA molecule used to carry an inserted sequence into a host.
The regulatory and cellular context that allows a gene’s product to be made.

Join a sequence with a carrier

Genetic engineering can assemble DNA from different sources. A vector carries a sequence into a host where it may be maintained and expressed. Plasmids are one type of vector; they are small DNA molecules separate from the main bacterial chromosome.

Restriction enzymes recognize particular DNA sequences and cut the backbone. Some cuts leave overhanging “sticky ends” that can pair with complementary ends. seals the backbone connections to form a joined molecule.

Matching ends help the pieces fit, but simply mixing DNA is not enough to guarantee the correct arrangement or a functional product.

Make the information usable by the host

A transferred gene must be linked to appropriate expression signals and interpreted by the host machinery. Many human genes contain introns. Bacteria do not normally process human introns in the same way as human cells, so a suitable intron-free coding sequence may be used.

Complementary DNA, or cDNA, can be made from a processed RNA template. This provides one route to an intron-free sequence. The conceptual point is that the host must receive usable coding information, not just any piece cut from a human chromosome.

Production of a human protein in bacteria therefore depends on both the sequence and the expression context. The insulin example illustrates a biological manufacturing principle rather than a complete laboratory protocol.

Verify several different claims

Finding an insert shows that DNA is present. Detecting its RNA supports transcription. Detecting the intended protein supports expression, while demonstrating its biological activity tests function. These are related but distinct claims.

A useful evaluation asks what was changed, what product was measured, how it was compared with a control and whether unintended effects were examined. Avoid treating “genetically modified” as a single guaranteed outcome shared by all organisms and technologies.

Use the mechanism to interpret evidence. Do not infer safety, effectiveness or environmental performance solely from a technology’s name.

Worked example

DNA presence is not protein function

A host contains an inserted coding sequence, but no protein measurement is provided.

  1. The DNA result supports successful presence of the insert.
  2. It does not establish that the host transcribed or translated it.
  3. Further measurements would be needed to demonstrate the intended protein and its function.
  4. A compatible regulatory context helps explain why insertion and expression are different steps.

Chapter 18 · printed pp. 655–660

Open p. 655 · Open p. 660

Key terms: · · ·

Vocabulary help

Key terms

Words for this lesson

Use these definitions when you need help with a term.

A method that amplifies a selected DNA region through repeated cycles.
Separation of molecules by movement through a gel under an electric field.
A set of DNA fragments of known sizes used as a reference in a gel.
A pattern based on selected variable DNA regions used for comparison.

Amplify a selected region

increases the amount of a selected DNA region. Repeated cycles separate the strands, allow primers to bind, and use a heat-stable to extend new strands. Primers define the region to be copied.

In an idealized model, each complete cycle doubles the number of target molecules. Starting from one target molecule, three ideal cycles produce eight. Real reactions may not double perfectly throughout, so the model is a calculation aid rather than a guarantee about every experiment.

Read a gel from wells toward the positive end

DNA has a negative charge because of its phosphate backbone. In a standard DNA gel, an electric field draws fragments toward the positive electrode. Smaller fragments usually travel farther through the gel than larger fragments under the same conditions.

Samples are loaded into separate lanes. A provides fragments of known sizes for comparison. Identify the wells, migration direction and ladder before interpreting a band position.

A band represents many molecules of similar length, not one whole cell. Two fragments can have the same length without necessarily having identical sequences.

Compare patterns without overstating identity

DNA profiling compares selected markers rather than reading every in the genome. In a simplified classroom matching problem, compare the complete supplied pattern, not just one shared band. Excluding a sample that lacks required bands differs from proving every circumstance associated with a compatible sample.

In a simplified parentage exercise, each child marker must be explainable by inheritance from the proposed parents. Account for the maternal contributions before comparing the remaining markers with possible paternal contributions.

Actual interpretation also considers laboratory quality, contamination, relatedness and statistical evidence. A classroom gel cannot by itself establish guilt, consent or the circumstances in which material was deposited.

Worked example

Read distance as fragment size

In one lane, band A remains near the wells and band B travels farther toward the positive electrode.

  1. Identify the wells as the loading end.
  2. Confirm that DNA moved toward the positive electrode.
  3. Under the same run conditions, the farther band B corresponds to smaller fragments than A.
  4. Use a ladder to estimate sizes; distance alone does not identify the full sequence.

Practise with support

Apply the explanation

Try both questions. Use the hint to revise your thinking after an incorrect answer.

Try this before opening the explanation

Show the explanation

Chapter 18 · printed pp. 660–661

Open p. 660 · Open p. 661

Key terms: · · ·

Vocabulary help

Key terms

Words for this lesson

Use these definitions when you need help with a term.

Determining the order of nucleotides in a DNA molecule.
Producing genetically very similar copies of a DNA molecule, cell or organism by a specified method.
An intervention intended to change, replace or alter the use of genetic information.
A boundary on what a study or observation can establish.

Identify what the technology actually does

Sequencing determines base order. increases copies of a selected region. Recombinant-DNA methods assemble genetic material, while may refer to copies of DNA, cells or whole organisms. These terms are related but not interchangeable.

A proposed might replace missing function, alter expression or change a sequence in target cells. Its success depends on reaching the appropriate cells, achieving the intended change and avoiding unacceptable unintended effects.

A result in one cell type or experimental system cannot automatically be generalized to every tissue or organism.

Separate a measured result from a broad claim

Suppose a hypothetical intervention increases production of a protein in cultured cells. That supports a change in expression under those conditions. It does not alone demonstrate improved organ function, long-term benefit or acceptable safety in a whole organism.

A stronger evaluation would ask about comparison groups, reproducibility, functional measurements, unintended changes and duration. These are questions about the evidence needed, not a prediction that every promising technology will succeed or fail.

The examples here teach how to evaluate mechanisms and claims. They are not recommendations for personal testing, treatment or laboratory work.

Include people and environments in the question

Genetic information can affect individuals and biological relatives. Research and applications raise questions about informed consent, privacy, access and how benefits and uncertainties are communicated. Environmental applications also require evidence about the affected populations and ecological setting.

A clear response distinguishes scientific findings from value-based choices. Explain what a technology does, what outcomes have actually been measured in the supplied case, and what remains unknown. Do not replace evidence with either enthusiasm about a label or fear of the label.

No personal DNA or family medical information is required for these activities.

Worked example

Evaluate a culture-to-organ claim

A hypothetical company observes increased enzyme production in a dish and advertises that it has restored normal organ function.

  1. The measured result is enzyme production in cultured cells.
  2. The advertised conclusion concerns whole-organ function, a different level.
  3. Ask for evidence that the enzyme is functional and that relevant tissue processes improve.
  4. Long-term and unintended effects also need evaluation.
  5. The culture result can be useful without supporting the complete advertised claim.

Practise with support

Apply the explanation

Try both questions. Use the hint to revise your thinking after an incorrect answer.

Stop and think

Try this before opening the explanation

Show the explanation

No. It defines the scope of the result and what still needs testing.

Can you connect a DNA sequence with its copying, expression and evidence?

Learning goal

Integrate molecular mechanisms, sequence reasoning and interpretation of technology results.

Before you begin

Optional embedded reading

Chapter 18 · printed pp. 663–665

Open p. 663 · Open p. 665

Key terms: · · ·

Vocabulary help

Key terms

Words for this lesson

Use these definitions when you need help with a term.

The DNA strand read by RNA polymerase to construct complementary RNA.
A three-nucleotide sequence in mRNA interpreted during translation.
A persistent change in a DNA sequence.
A pattern based on selected variable DNA regions used for comparison.

How to complete this section

  1. Use the summary and synthesis example to find any mechanisms you need to revisit.
  2. Try the optional independent set before opening its feedback.
  3. Open the required final check and select Start. Correct six selections, save both written explanations, then select Submit and finish.
  4. Find earlier attempts and later practice in All My Work.

Expected work: one completed final-check run. The independent set and textbook review are optional.

Follow information without confusing the molecules

Replication copies DNA through complementary semiconservative synthesis. Transcription uses one template to make RNA, and translation reads mRNA codons to assemble a polypeptide. RNA processing modifies the message without normally deleting introns from the genomic DNA.

A sequence answer should identify the strand and direction, preserve antiparallel pairing and use the correct reading frame. A stop codon is a signal, not an amino acid.

Connect a change with the relevant measurement

A DNA mutation may alter a product, but its effect must be traced through the sequence and biological context. Recombination can create new combinations without a new mutation at every locus.

PCR, gels, sequencing and recombinant-DNA methods provide different kinds of evidence. A complete explanation identifies what each method measures and separates compatibility, expression and function from stronger unsupported claims.

Connect the main ideas

TopicWhat you should be able to explain
Evidence that DNA carries genetic informationConnect each experiment with its observation, control and justified conclusion.
DNA structure and complementary strandsIdentify nucleotide components, complementary base pairing and antiparallel strand directions.
DNA replication and its productsTrace semiconservative replication using base pairing, enzyme roles and the 5′ to 3′ synthesis rule.
Genes, RNA and the flow of informationDistinguish DNA storage from RNA and protein roles, and explain selective gene expression.
Transcription and RNA processingUse template and coding strand identities to construct mRNA and explain eukaryotic RNA processing.
Translation and the genetic codeUse mRNA codons, tRNA anticodons and start/stop signals to explain polypeptide synthesis.
Solving DNA, RNA and protein problemsSolve sequence problems by identifying the supplied molecule, direction, frame and requested output.
Mutations and their effects on proteinsDistinguish a DNA mutation from expression errors and explain substitution, frameshift and inheritance consequences.
Recombination and sources of variationDistinguish mutation, recombination and transfer of existing genetic material.
Recombinant DNA and genetic engineeringExplain the conceptual roles of restriction enzymes, ligase, vectors and expression in recombinant-DNA technology.
PCR, gels and interpreting DNA profilesExplain DNA amplification and fragment separation, then interpret profiles within their limits.
Genetic technologies and evidence-based decisionsCompare sequencing, cloning and gene-based interventions by their mechanism, evidence and limits.

Worked example

Trace a sequence change without overstating its effect

Coding DNA changes from 5′-ATG CAA TAA-3′ to 5′-ATG CAG TAA-3′.

  1. The corresponding RNA changes CAA to CAG in the second codon.
  2. Both CAA and CAG specify glutamine.
  3. Both simplified messages produce Met–Gln, then stop.
  4. Classify the substitution’s amino-acid effect as silent.
  5. Do not infer an organism-level effect without additional context or measurements.

Optional extension

Biotechnology and unintended consequences

How can a useful intended effect be evaluated alongside other effects?

A bounded hypothetical case

A hypothetical plant line is engineered to produce a protein that reduces feeding by one insect. In a controlled plot, leaf damage is lower than in an otherwise comparable line. No measurements of other organisms or long-term population changes are supplied.

The result supports reduced damage in the tested conditions. It does not yet answer every question about ecological effects or performance elsewhere.

Identify the next evidence

An evaluation can distinguish the intended trait from unintended changes, compare appropriate controls and consider effects on other organisms. The important measurements depend on the proposed use and exposure.

This is a paper-based evidence exercise. It does not ask you to grow modified organisms or to make a policy decision from incomplete information.

Compare after saving your explanation

Reduced leaf damage was observed under the tested conditions. Measurements of non-target organisms and longer-term population or environmental outcomes would address broader effects. Appropriate comparisons and replication are needed; the short plot result should not be treated as universal evidence of either safety or harm.

Mixed practice

How to use mixed practice
  1. Choose a topic and set size, then select Start practice.
  2. Read each task: some ask for a term, some for a selection, and some for a sequence.
  3. For a sequence, choose each step once and put the steps in biological order.
  4. Use the feedback, continue through the set, and select Submit and finish.

How to complete textbook practicechoose question → read → show your process → save

Paper work is not stored by this course. Include labels, units and every required part. Use only supplied diagrams or data for analysis activities; do not perform the investigation procedures shown on a source page.

Core Vocabulary

Use each term to explain a relationship, not just repeat a definition.

How to use vocabulary and Frayer work
  1. Search the chapter terms or select a topic.
  2. Open a definition for its meaning, example and important distinction.
  3. Choose up to eight words for your Frayer work. Each chapter keeps a separate selection.
  4. Complete four responses per word, with 240 characters maximum per response.
  5. Select Collect this word. Editing it later returns it to draft status.
  6. After completing your own four valid responses, open the course model to compare. Print your work from All My Work.

Overlong Frayer text is not saved until shortened. No student answer is prefilled. Scientific accuracy is not automatically graded.
